meta.title: R1 research studio: what makes a question worth researching? Questions, rewrites, exemplars and checks
meta.built_by: by hand for curriculum v2 §11 (R1); question types and templates from §11.2; rubric from §3.4 (assets/learn/components/rubric.js)
meta.note: The twenty questions, the rewrites, the co-op, Prairie Town, Prairie City and the exemplars are illustrative. Two answers quote public numbers, with their sources below.

bins.label: Not answerable with the data at hand
bins.sub: the data named cannot show it

questions.text: In 2025, how many hours did Prairie Town's wind output stay below a tenth of its maximum, season by season?
questions.why: Specific and answerable: the town's hourly 2025 wind data can be counted by season.
questions.typeWhy: Descriptive: it asks how often, not why.

questions.text: Is solar power good?
questions.why: Good for whom, measured how, compared with what? No audience, metric or comparison.

questions.text: How much electricity did the United States use in 2025?
questions.why: EIA publishes it: about 4.20 trillion kWh. A lookup, not a study; why use changed could be one.

questions.text: Did a co-op's time-of-use tariff cut its members' evening peak demand, compared with similar co-ops that kept flat rates?
questions.why: A named programme, a metric and a comparison group.
questions.typeWhy: Evaluative: it judges a past change against a comparison.

questions.text: Using only each state's yearly electricity sales, at what hour of the day do electric-vehicle owners charge?
questions.why: Yearly totals cannot show hours. Hourly charger or feeder data could.

questions.text: What mix of rooftop solar and batteries should a school district buy to keep its 20-year cost lowest, compared with grid supply alone?
questions.why: A decision-maker, a metric and a comparison, with public prices and tariffs to work from.
questions.typeWhy: Prescriptive: it asks what a decision-maker should do.

questions.text: How can we fix the grid?
questions.why: Fix what: outages, prices, emissions? Which grid, and who would act?

questions.text: Why did heating demand fall more in some neighbourhoods than in others after the same retrofit programme?
questions.why: An observed difference to explain, with meter and building data to test the reasons.
questions.typeWhy: Explanatory: it asks why an observed difference happened.

questions.text: Does a battery give back less energy than it takes in?
questions.why: Yes: every charge and discharge loses some energy (round-trip efficiency, lesson 9). How much one battery loses can still be measured.

questions.text: During a week-long cold snap, how would all-electric heating change the risk of elderly households losing heat, with and without backup?
questions.why: A stated event, a group, a risk to estimate and two cases to compare.
questions.typeWhy: Predictive: it asks what would happen under a stated event, with uncertainty.

questions.text: Where in Prairie City are rooftop solar systems concentrated, compared with median household income by neighbourhood?
questions.why: Specific and answerable from permit records and census income data.
questions.typeWhy: Descriptive: it maps where, without asking why.

questions.text: What is the future of energy storage?
questions.why: No place, period, metric or audience: a topic, not a question.

questions.text: Using one year of a utility's outage records, how will its customers' outage hours change by 2060?
questions.why: One year cannot separate a trend from a bad year, and 2060 needs scenarios as well as records.

questions.text: Did a rural co-op's community-solar programme lower renters' energy burden more than bill credits of the same cost would have?
questions.why: A programme, a metric and a fair counterfactual: the same money spent another way.
questions.typeWhy: Evaluative: it judges a past programme against an alternative.

questions.text: What was the average capacity factor of U.S. utility-scale wind farms in 2025?
questions.why: EIA reports it: 33.8% (Electric Power Monthly). Why regions differ could be a study.

questions.text: What will Prairie City's winter peak demand be in 2035 if half its homes switch to heat pumps, and with what range?
questions.why: A stated change, a metric with units and a range to estimate.
questions.typeWhy: Predictive: it asks what a future value will be, with uncertainty.

questions.text: Are heat pumps worth it?
questions.why: Worth what, to whom, over how long, compared with which heating?

questions.text: Which pumping schedule should a Plains farm adopt to cut its power bill under the co-op's time-of-use tariff without lowering yield?
questions.why: A decision, a goal and a limit, with the tariff and pump data to work from.
questions.typeWhy: Prescriptive: it asks what the farm should do.

questions.text: Using Prairie Town's hourly grid demand alone, why did each household's electricity use change?
questions.why: Town-level demand mixes thousands of homes; household changes need meter data or a survey.

questions.text: Why did some rural co-ops' customers lose power for longer than their neighbours' in the same ice storm?
questions.why: An observed difference, with outage records and line data to test the reasons.
questions.typeWhy: Explanatory: it asks why the same storm had different effects.

example.question: Did the co-op's community-solar array lower members' average yearly bill, compared with buying the same energy at wholesale prices?
example.audience: the co-op's board, which decides whether to build a second array
example.counterfactual: the same energy bought at wholesale prices

example.question: Over 15 years, would a cold-climate heat pump cost a Prairie Town homeowner less than a new gas furnace?
example.audience: homeowners replacing a furnace, and the town's rebate office
example.counterfactual: a new gas furnace installed at the same time

rewrites.vague: How can we fix the grid?

example.question: Which would cut Prairie Town's customer outage hours more per dollar over ten years: a second feeder or a battery at the substation?
example.metric: customer outage hours avoided per $1 million spent
example.counterfactual: today's single feeder, with no upgrade

rubric.title: Rate your card against the rubric
rubric.lede: The course rubric's own words. R1 builds one competence of nine: framing.

competences.look: your card passes all eight checks, and its boundary says what is left out.

rubric.note: Your rating stays in this browser. A studio is practice, not a certificate: the course's readiness claim also needs the checkpoints and a research capstone.

exemplars.title: Two cards for the same vague question
exemplars.task: Turn “Is community solar good for low-income families?” into a question card.

parts.note: “Good” is not a metric: any result could be read as success.
Without a type, a survey, a model and a regression could all claim to answer it.
No units and no period: dollars a month, or a share of income, over which years?
A place, not a [[system-boundary|boundary]]: which programme, which members, which years, and what is left out?
No falsification statement: no result could show the expectation wrong.

answers.label: Strong answer
parts:
Question: Did a rural co-op's community-solar programme lower renters' energy burden more than bill credits of the same cost would have?
Type:

parts.note: Names the type: a past programme judged against a comparison.
Names who would act on the answer.

parts.text: yearly energy bills as % of household income
parts.note: A metric with units that bills and income data can compute.

parts.text: bill credits of the same total cost
parts.note: The counterfactual spends the same money another way, so the comparison is fair.

parts.text: the co-op's renter members, 2022–2025; landlords' costs left out
parts.note: Says who and which years are counted, and what is left out.

parts.text: participants' burden fell no more than that of similar renters given credits
parts.note: Names the result that would show the expectation false.

parts: Main uncertainty: renters who moved away during the four years

diff.label: Boundary
diff.good: Members, years, what is left out

diff.label: Falsification
diff.good: A result that would show it wrong

exemplars.note: Both cards are illustrative: the co-op and its programme are invented. Tap a marked phrase to read its note.

checklist.label: One sentence
checklist.text: About one system and one period, ending in a question mark.

checklist.label: Typed
checklist.text: Descriptive, explanatory, evaluative, predictive or prescriptive.

checklist.label: Audience
checklist.text: Someone who would act on the answer, or read it.

checklist.label: Metric with units
checklist.text: Something you could measure or compute, such as [[energy-burden|energy burden]] in % of income.

checklist.label: Counterfactual
checklist.text: What happens otherwise: the baseline you compare with.

checklist.label: Still open
checklist.text: Not a lookup in a public dataset, and not settled physics.

checklist.label: Answerable
checklist.text: Data you can get show the effect, at the time step it needs.

checklist.label: Falsifiable
checklist.text: You can name a result that would show you wrong.
